title: A Gate That Needs Two Signals

scenes.tts: A synapse must know that its input fired, and that its own cell is active. What molecule could read both?
scenes.visual: A spine with a question mark; arrows labelled input and cell point at it.
scenes.narration: A synapse must know that its input fired, and that its own cell is active. What molecule could read both?

scenes.tts: Look at one synapse, from C A three onto C A one. The terminal releases glutamate onto a spine, a small bud on the dendrite.
scenes.caption: Look at one synapse, from CA3 onto CA1. The terminal releases glutamate onto a spine, a small bud on the dendrite.
scenes.visual: Zoom from the hippocampus map to one Schaffer terminal facing a spine on a CA1 dendrite. Glutamate dots spill into the cleft.
scenes.narration: Look at one synapse, from CA3 onto CA1. The terminal releases glutamate onto a spine, a small bud on the dendrite.

scenes.tts: Two kinds of ionotropic glutamate receptor sit there.
scenes.visual: Two receptor shapes on the spine, one blue (AMPA), one orange (NMDA).
scenes.narration: Two kinds of ionotropic glutamate receptor sit there.

scenes.tts: AMPA receptors need only glutamate to open. They carry most of the ordinary E P S P.
scenes.caption: AMPA receptors need only glutamate to open. They carry most of the ordinary EPSP.
scenes.visual: Glutamate binds the blue receptor; it opens and sodium flows in. Label: AMPA, needs only glutamate, carries the ordinary EPSP.
scenes.narration: AMPA receptors need only glutamate to open. They carry most of the ordinary EPSP.

scenes.tts: N M D A receptors also bind glutamate. They need a co-agonist too, glycine or D serine, which is normally present.
scenes.caption: NMDA receptors also bind glutamate. They need a co-agonist too, glycine or D-serine, which is normally present.
scenes.visual: Glutamate and a small co-agonist bind the orange receptor. Label: NMDA, needs glycine or D-serine.
scenes.narration: NMDA receptors also bind glutamate. They need a co-agonist too, glycine or D-serine, which is normally present.

scenes.tts: But at rest, a magnesium ion from outside sits in their pore and blocks it.
scenes.visual: A green Mg2+ ball lodges in the orange pore. Nothing passes.
scenes.narration: But at rest, a magnesium ion from outside sits in their pore and blocks it.

scenes.tts: Once the block clears, they pass sodium, potassium and calcium.
scenes.visual: The Mg2+ ball leaves; Na+, K+ and Ca2+ icons pass through the pore.
scenes.narration: Once the block clears, they pass sodium, potassium and calcium.

scenes.tts: What clears the block? Depolarization. Magnesium is positive, held in by the negative inside. Make the inside less negative, and it is pushed out.
scenes.visual: The inside of the spine shades from deep negative to less negative; the Mg2+ ball drifts outward and pops free.
scenes.narration: What clears the block? Depolarization. Magnesium is positive, held in by the negative inside. Make the inside less negative, and it is pushed out.

scenes.tts: Where does the depolarization come from? Recall the balance point from the action potential lesson. It works like a tug of war.
scenes.visual: The voltage scale from the action potential lesson slides in, with its marker and ropes.
scenes.narration: Where does the depolarization come from? Recall the balance point from the action potential lesson. It works like a tug of war.

scenes.tts: Take an isolated compartment, with fixed ohmic conductances, and no injected or axial current. Its voltage relaxes toward a weighted average. Each current's reversal potential counts in proportion to its conductance.
scenes.visual: On screen: V∞ = Σg·E / Σg; isolated compartment, fixed ohmic conductances, no injected or axial current. The rope with more open channels pulls the marker closer to its own end.
scenes.narration: Take an isolated compartment, with fixed ohmic conductances, and no injected or axial current. Its voltage relaxes toward a weighted average. Each current's reversal potential counts in proportion to its conductance.
scenes.caption: Take an isolated compartment, with fixed ohmic conductances, and no injected or axial current. Its voltage relaxes toward a weighted average. Each current's reversal potential counts in proportion to its conductance.

scenes.tts: AMPA current reverses near zero millivolts. When many receptors open at once, they pull the local balance point up from near minus 70.
scenes.caption: AMPA current reverses near 0 mV. When many receptors open at once, they pull the local balance point up from near −70 mV.
scenes.visual: A new blue rope labelled AMPA reversal ≈ 0 mV thickens as more receptors open, and drags the marker up from −70 mV.
scenes.narration: AMPA current reverses near 0 mV. When many receptors open at once, they pull the local balance point up from near −70 mV.

scenes.tts: A spike fired by the cell and spreading back into the dendrite also depolarizes the spine.
scenes.visual: A spike starts at the axon initial segment, invades the cell body and sweeps back up the dendrite into the spine.
scenes.narration: A spike fired by the cell and spreading back into the dendrite also depolarizes the spine.

scenes.tts: So the spine voltage reports what the postsynaptic cell is doing. And the magnesium block reads that voltage. A spike is one source of depolarization, not the only one.
scenes.visual: The spine's voltage meter rises; the Mg2+ ball responds by leaving the pore.
scenes.narration: So the spine voltage reports what the postsynaptic cell is doing. And the magnesium block reads that voltage. A spike is one source of depolarization, not the only one.

scenes.tts: Now put the signals together, as a product of three factors. First, glutamate must be bound. Second, depolarization clears the block. Third, calcium still needs an inward push.
scenes.visual: Formula box: Ca2+ entry through NMDA receptors ∝ (glutamate bound) × (fraction of block cleared) × (inward push on Ca2+). Small note: steady-flux model; Jahr–Stevens block × GHK Ca2+ flux; 1 mM external Mg2+, 2 mM external Ca2+, 100 nM internal Ca2+, 35 °C; ligand activation fixed, co-agonist present.
scenes.narration: Now put the signals together, as a product of three factors. First, glutamate must be bound. Second, depolarization clears the block. Third, calcium still needs an inward push.

scenes.tts: The active terminal supplies glutamate. The other two factors are set by the voltage of the postsynaptic membrane.
scenes.visual: The glutamate factor is tagged active terminal; the block and push factors are tagged postsynaptic voltage.
scenes.narration: The active terminal supplies glutamate. The other two factors are set by the voltage of the postsynaptic membrane.

scenes.tts: With no glutamate, no calcium enters through these receptors, at any voltage. That makes the N M D A receptor a coincidence detector.
scenes.caption: With no glutamate, no calcium enters through these receptors, at any voltage. That makes the NMDA receptor a coincidence detector.
scenes.visual: A voltage slider sweeps across with no glutamate present; the meter labelled Ca2+ through NMDA receptors stays at zero. Label: coincidence detector.
scenes.narration: With no glutamate, no calcium enters through these receptors, at any voltage. That makes the NMDA receptor a coincidence detector.

scenes.tts: Near rest, with glutamate bound, about one receptor in twenty is unblocked. Depolarize the spine, and about one in three is.
scenes.visual: A two-by-two table fills in: no glutamate rows read no Ca2+; glutamate at −70 mV reads about 1 in 20 unblocked; at −30 mV, about 1 in 3, about 4 times more Ca2+. Footnote: illustrative model, 1 mM external Mg2+, 2 mM external Ca2+, 100 nM internal Ca2+, 35 °C.
scenes.narration: Near rest, with glutamate bound, about one receptor in twenty is unblocked. Depolarize the spine, and about one in three is.

scenes.tts: Glutamate arrives at a spine sitting near rest. Does any calcium get in?
scenes.visual: A spine at −70 mV; glutamate arrives. A question mark over the Ca2+ meter.
scenes.narration: Glutamate arrives at a spine sitting near rest. Does any calcium get in?

scenes.tts: A little. The gate is graded, not a switch. Even at rest a few receptors are unblocked, so glutamate alone lets in a trickle.
scenes.visual: A few of many NMDA receptors are unplugged; a thin trickle of Ca2+ enters.
scenes.narration: A little. The gate is graded, not a switch. Even at rest a few receptors are unblocked, so glutamate alone lets in a trickle.

scenes.tts: And more depolarization is not always better. In this model, with normal magnesium, calcium entry through the receptor peaks near minus 20 millivolts, then falls.
scenes.caption: And more depolarization is not always better. In this model, with normal magnesium, calcium entry through the receptor peaks near −20 mV, then falls.
scenes.visual: A curve labelled NMDA-mediated Ca2+ influx rate, illustrative model (1 mM Mg2+), rises from −70 mV, peaks near −20 mV and falls toward +40 mV.
scenes.narration: And more depolarization is not always better. In this model, with normal magnesium, calcium entry through the receptor peaks near −20 mV, then falls.

scenes.tts: That is the third factor. Depolarization weakens the inward push on calcium.
scenes.visual: An inward arrow on Ca2+ shrinks as the voltage marker moves up.
scenes.narration: That is the third factor. Depolarization weakens the inward push on calcium.

scenes.tts: So for the same receptor, minus 30 instead of minus 70 speeds calcium entry only about four times. Where does the big difference come from?
scenes.caption: So for the same receptor, −30 instead of −70 mV speeds calcium entry only about four times. Where does the big difference come from?
scenes.visual: On screen: same receptor, −30 vs −70 mV: about 4 times the Ca2+ entry rate (steady model).
scenes.narration: So for the same receptor, −30 instead of −70 mV speeds calcium entry only about four times. Where does the big difference come from?

scenes.tts: Mainly from summation. During a fast train, glutamate keeps arriving faster than the receptors close. And the depolarization builds.
scenes.visual: A 100 Hz train: glutamate pulses stack up before receptors close; the spine voltage ratchets upward.
scenes.narration: Mainly from summation. During a fast train, glutamate keeps arriving faster than the receptors close. And the depolarization builds.

scenes.tts: The receptors stay activated while the responses summate, and the calcium in the spine climbs steeply.
scenes.visual: The Ca2+ meter in the spine climbs steeply.
scenes.narration: The receptors stay activated while the responses summate, and the calcium in the spine climbs steeply.

scenes.tts: The takeaway: at normal magnesium levels, an N M D A receptor lets in much calcium only when glutamate and depolarization coincide.
scenes.caption: The takeaway: at normal magnesium levels, an NMDA receptor lets in much calcium only when glutamate and depolarization coincide.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: at normal extracellular Mg2+, much Ca2+ through NMDA receptors only when glutamate and depolarization coincide.
scenes.narration: The takeaway: at normal magnesium levels, an NMDA receptor lets in much calcium only when glutamate and depolarization coincide.
